retrieved.title: CrashLoopBackOff
retrieved.text:
## Fixes

- If the command is wrong (for example a demo container that ends in `exit 1`), correct `command`/`args` or the image entrypoint so the main process stays in the foreground.
- If a config value is missing, add the env var or volume and roll the workload.
- If a dependency is down, fix that service or make startup retry instead of exiting.
- If a liveness probe is too aggressive, increase `initialDelaySeconds` / `failureThreshold` (see probe-failures).
- After a fix, roll the deployment and confirm the restart count stops climbing:

  ```bash
  kubectl rollout status deploy/<name> -n <ns>
  kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> --watch
  ```

retrieved.title: CreateContainerError
retrieved.text:
## Symptoms

- Pod is `Waiting` with reason `CreateContainerError`.
- Events include `Failed` from the kubelet with a runtime error (device mapper, `no space left on device`, seccomp / AppArmor / SELinux denial, invalid capability, or a missing device plugin).
- The image has often already been pulled (`ImagePullBackOff` is not the current reason).
- Application logs are typically unavailable because the container never started.

retrieved.title: CreateContainerError
retrieved.text:
## Common causes

- The node disk is full, so the runtime cannot create the container's writable layer.
- A security context asks for a capability, seccomp profile, AppArmor profile, or user that the node or policy will not allow.
- A device plugin (GPU, FPGA) is required but not healthy, or the requested resource is gone.
- An invalid `command` / working directory / symlink inside the image, or a corrupted image snapshot.
- Runtime bugs or leftover half-created containers after a kubelet crash.

retrieved.title: CreateContainerConfigError
retrieved.text:
## Symptoms

- Pod is `Pending` or `Waiting` with reason `CreateContainerConfigError`.
- Events include `Failed` with a message such as `Error: secret "..." not found`, `couldn't find key ... in ConfigMap ...`, or `configmap "..." not found`.
- Restart count is usually zero. `kubectl logs` will fail or return an "unavailable" message.

retrieved.title: Liveness and readiness probe failures
retrieved.text:
## Diagnosis

1. Inspect the probe definitions and recent probe events:

   ```bash
   kubectl describe pod <pod> -n <ns>
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].livenessProbe}'
   kubectl get pod <pod> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].readinessProbe}'
   kubectl get endpoints <svc> -n <ns>
   ```

2. Exec into a running container (if it lives long enough) and call the same path or command the probe uses.
3. Read current and previous logs around the time of each restart. If the process is killed mid-startup, the liveness probe is a prime suspect.
4. Distinguish "app is crashing on its own" (see CrashLoopBackOff) from "kubelet is killing a healthy-but-slow process".
